questions.question: You join a team as a senior engineer and inherit a service with 4 years of accumulated technical debt — flaky tests, unclear ownership, painful deploys, and 3 AM pages twice a week. Walk me through your first 90 days.
questions.title: Scenario: Senior Engineer's First 90 Days on a High-Debt, High-Incident Team
questions.direct_answer: **First 30 days: observe, don't fix.** Shadow on-call, read ADRs and postmortems (or write the first ones), pair with every teammate, trace a real request end-to-end, and produce a **written assessment** — the biggest risks, the quickest wins, the structural problems — reviewed with the team and manager. **Days 30–60: stabilize the bleeding.** Attack the top 2–3 pain points (flaky tests, deploy pain, noisiest alert) with small visible wins; start an ADR habit; set up a postmortem cadence; fix one runbook per incident. **Days 60–90: structural investment.** Begin a named debt-reduction track (15–20% of team capacity), establish SLOs and an error budget, introduce design reviews for new work, and start a measurable north-star (MTTR, deploy frequency, flaky-test rate, or DORA metrics). Throughout: **build relationships**, never blame the team for the state they inherited, escalate with data not drama, and resist the hero urge (fixing things alone doesn't scale — fixing the system does). Red flags to watch for: a team that can't say no to product, a manager who wants the problem "just solved", and untouchable sacred cows that are actually the root cause.

interviewer_intent.soft_skills: Judgment, prioritization, patience, leadership, systems thinking, relationship-building
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Charging in with rewrites; heroics instead of systems; blaming the team; fixing symptoms not root causes
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Structured 30/60/90 plan, observation-first, measurable north-stars, debt-reduction track, SLO/error budget, escalation with data

sections.title: The Scenario and What's Really Being Asked
sections.content:
**The situation:** You've joined a team as a senior engineer. Inherited reality:
- A critical service with 4 years of accumulated debt
- Flaky CI (30% of PRs need re-runs)
- Deploys take 2 hours and often roll back
- On-call is burning people out (2 pages a week at 3 AM, several false positives)
- No ADRs, vague ownership, tribal knowledge, scattered runbooks
- Product pressure is intense; the team hasn't shipped a major feature in two quarters

**What the interviewer is testing**
- Do you act with humility (observe first) or ego (rewrite immediately)?
- Can you distinguish symptoms (flaky tests) from root causes (no test ownership, no CI isolation)?
- Do you build a **system** that compounds, or heroically fix one thing?
- Can you communicate with management, product, and the team all at once?
- Do you escalate sensibly when necessary?
- Do you measure impact, or just feel busy?

**What separates good from great answers**
- A structured, time-bounded plan (30/60/90)
- Specific metrics and north-stars
- Awareness of the human dynamics (burnout, cynicism, political risk)
- Willingness to escalate cleanly with data
- Humility: no one wakes up wanting technical debt; ask why it got this way before judging

sections.title: Days 0–30: Observe, Diagnose, Build Trust
sections.content:
**Rule: don't change anything major in the first 30 days** (except obvious security or critical-bleed fixes).

**Listen tour**
- 30-min 1:1 with every teammate: what's working, what's broken, what would you change if you had a magic wand, what are you afraid to say in group settings
- 1:1 with manager: their goals, fears, boundaries, what success looks like for them
- 1:1 with product counterpart: their roadmap, frustrations, trust level
- 1:1 with adjacent teams: platform, SRE, security, partner services — what's it like working with this team?
- Write notes after each conversation; look for patterns

**Shadow on-call**
- Sit with the on-call for a full week
- Track every page: what was it, how was it fixed, was there a runbook, how long did it take
- Categorize pages: real issues vs. noise vs. missing runbook vs. known-but-ignored

**Read the history**
- Last 20 postmortems (write the first ones if none exist)
- Last 50 PRs and their review comments — tone? depth? pattern?
- ADRs, design docs, anything written down
- Git log — who touches what; where's the churn

**Trace a real request end-to-end**
- Pick the most-common real user action
- Follow it through every service, every queue, every DB, every cache
- Note the painful parts: the hand-offs, the missing logs, the magic config
- This tells you more about the system than any doc

**Quick wins (that cost nothing)**
- Fix one obvious typo or stale doc per day — builds momentum without threat
- Clean up a top-10 flaky test with a clear root cause
- Add logging to the part of the request flow that's dark
- These show competence without claiming authority

**Produce a written assessment (end of week 4)**
- **Top risks**: what will bite us in the next 90 days without intervention
- **Quick wins**: 3–5 things we can fix in the next 30 days with high impact
- **Structural issues**: things that need investment and trade-offs
- **Relationships and dynamics**: where trust is good, where it's strained
- Share with manager first; then the team; then adjacent leaders
- **Frame as questions and proposals, not judgments** — you're still new

sections.title: Days 30–60: Stabilize the Bleeding
sections.content:
Now with context and team buy-in, attack the 2–3 highest-pain, highest-feasibility issues.

**Flaky tests**
- Set up a flaky-test dashboard (Datadog CI, GitHub Actions custom, or open source like Trunk)
- Quarantine top-10 flaky tests immediately; open tickets with owners
- Root-cause fix them one per week; require tests to be stable for 2 weeks before re-enabling
- **Make it policy**: a test that flakes twice in a week gets quarantined automatically
- **Measure**: flaky-test rate should drop from 30% to <5% in 60 days

**Deploy pain**
- Audit the deploy pipeline stage-by-stage with timings
- Low-hanging fruit: parallelize independent stages, cache dependencies, smaller Docker images, skip unchanged-path tests
- Goal: cut deploy time 50% in 60 days
- Smoke tests automated post-deploy; rollback scripted, not manual
- **Deploy frequency target**: at least once a day, ideally more

**Noisy alerts**
- List every active alert; rate each: did it require human action last time it fired?
- Tune or delete the ones with <50% signal
- For those that remain, ensure each has a runbook (actionable, not "ping so-and-so")
- **Measure**: pages per week, % of pages that were actionable, MTTA (time to acknowledge), MTTR

**Install habits that compound**
- **Blameless postmortems**: every SEV-2+; a template; followed up on action items
- **ADR habit**: every non-trivial decision gets a one-pager in the repo
- **Runbook-per-alert**: no alert without a runbook; updated after every incident
- **Design review**: any new service, schema change, or externally visible change gets a 30-min async review before coding

**Talk about it publicly (internally)**
- Weekly team demo includes "what we fixed"
- Share the flaky-test dashboard in the team channel each Monday
- Visible progress builds morale and buys runway for structural work

**Escalate when needed**
- If product pressure is blocking stabilization, document the cost of the incident rate to the business
- Propose: 20% of team capacity on debt for 1 quarter, in exchange for specific velocity and reliability targets
- Frame as investment with a measurable return, not "we want to stop feature work"
- Loop manager and product lead together; shared message, same data

sections.title: Days 60–90: Structural Investment and North-Stars
sections.content:
Stabilization is visible; now lay the tracks for compounding improvement.

**Debt-reduction track (15–20% of capacity)**
- Named, scheduled, visible in the roadmap alongside features
- Prioritize by ROI: pain × frequency × fix cost
- Not a "someday" sink — planned work with owners and checkpoints
- Report impact each month: engineers hours saved, incidents avoided

**SLOs and error budgets**
- Define SLOs for the top 2–3 user journeys (latency p99, availability)
- Measure; show team what's currently happening
- When error budget is burnt, features pause in favor of reliability
- Creates a **shared language** with product for the trade-off

**Ownership clarity**
- Every service has a CODEOWNER, a primary on-call, a secondary, and a defined escalation path
- Service catalog (Backstage or lightweight equivalent)
- No orphaned code; if a service has no owner, escalate

**North-star metrics (DORA + local)**
- **Deploy frequency** (target: ≥1/day/team)
- **Lead time for change** (target: < 1 day)
- **Change failure rate** (target: < 15%)
- **MTTR** (target: < 1 hour for SEV-2)
- **Flaky-test rate** (target: < 5%)
- **Pages per on-call week** (target: < 3)
- Baseline them now; publish monthly; set quarterly targets

**Onboarding + knowledge sharing**
- Write / rewrite the onboarding doc (30/60/90 for new hires)
- Buddy system; curated first-PR list
- Brown-bags or guild participation; open office hours
- This prevents re-accumulating the same tribal-knowledge debt

**Design discipline**
- RFCs for anything multi-team or multi-quarter
- ADRs for any non-trivial decision
- 30-min async design review before major code is written
- Stops the flow of new debt at the source

**Team health**
- Check in with each person one more time at day 90
- Listen for burnout signs; negotiate on-call rotation, protected time
- Celebrate wins publicly; give credit generously
- Ensure the team feels the improvements are theirs, not yours

**Write a 90-day retrospective**
- What you expected, what you found, what you changed, what you'd do differently
- Share with your manager; useful for both your growth and org learning
- Honest about what you got wrong — that's how trust compounds

sections.title: Trade-offs, Failure Modes, and Senior Engineer Judgment
sections.content:
**Stabilize vs. rewrite**
- Tempting to propose rewriting everything; rarely right
- Rewrites take 2–3× longer than estimated, during which the existing system is starved of improvement
- Strangler pattern: improve the legacy while incrementally replacing
- Only rewrite when the system architecturally cannot meet future requirements, not merely because it's ugly

**Speed vs. process**
- Installing too much process too fast feels bureaucratic; team resists
- Too little process and improvements don't stick
- Start with 1–2 habits (ADRs + postmortems), add more only when current ones are alive

**Heroics vs. systems**
- You could fix the flaky tests in a weekend — don't
- Team watching you hero-fix doesn't learn the habit; fixes regress next quarter
- Pair with teammates, let them drive, teach the pattern

**Blame vs. learning**
- Easy to frame inherited mess as the team's failure
- Reality: they were under-resourced, under-prioritized, sometimes under-led
- Every postmortem blameless; every assessment respectful; no one wakes up wanting debt

**Escalation vs. patience**
- If product pressure keeps blocking stabilization, escalate with data
- But don't cry wolf: one clear, data-backed escalation earns credibility for future ones
- "We will have a SEV-1 in the next 45 days if we don't address X" — specific, falsifiable, actionable

**Sacred cows**
- Every high-debt codebase has untouchable pieces: an old framework, a well-loved-but-broken service, a person's pet project
- Sometimes those are the root cause
- Navigate carefully: data, allies, small wins, patience; don't die on every hill at once

**Common failure modes**
1. **The savior**: "I'll fix everything" — burns out, team stagnates, no compounding
2. **The judge**: criticizes the team before earning trust; becomes an outsider
3. **The firefighter**: always on the front line, never improves the system
4. **The rewriter**: proposes Big Bang rewrite; loses political capital in month 2
5. **The bureaucrat**: installs 5 new processes at once; team revolts
6. **The silent senior**: observes for 90 days and produces nothing; loses confidence
7. **The hero**: great solo output but team doesn't grow

**Senior engineer behaviors that work**
- **Observe first** — humility buys credibility
- **Write it down** — assessment, proposals, postmortems — leave artifacts
- **Measure baseline and progress** — data anchors trust
- **Pair and teach** — build team capability, not personal workload
- **Escalate cleanly** — private first, data, solution proposed
- **Credit team** — wins are theirs; you earn by multiplying, not claiming
- **Talk to product and management like partners** — shared incentives, not adversaries
- **Admit misjudgments publicly** — "I thought X, I was wrong because Y, here's what we'll do"

**Red flags to recognize**
- Manager wants "just fix it" without supporting investment → needs managing upward
- Product treats engineering as executor, not partner → needs relationship building
- Team has learned helplessness → needs visible wins + empowerment
- Sacred cows are actually root causes → needs patience + allies + data
- Escalation paths broken → document, escalate through your own manager with data

**When to leave**
- Rare but real: if the org is fundamentally unwilling to invest in engineering health
- After 6 months of honest effort with no structural support, it may be the system, not the job
- Leave cleanly; leave better than you found; don't scorched-earth

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **First 30 days: observe, don't fix** — listen tour, shadow on-call, read history, trace a real request, write an assessment
- **Days 30–60: stabilize the bleeding** — flaky tests, deploy time, noisy alerts; install postmortem + ADR + runbook habits
- **Days 60–90: structural investment** — debt track (15–20% capacity), SLOs/error budgets, ownership clarity, design reviews, north-star metrics
- **Measure**: DORA (deploy freq, lead time, change failure rate, MTTR), flaky-test rate, pages/week
- **Relationships first**: 1:1s with every teammate, manager, product, adjacent teams; no blaming
- **Escalate with data, not drama** — private first, solution proposed, shared message
- **Strangler, not rewrite** — incremental improvement beats Big Bang rewrite
- **Heroics don't scale** — build team capability through pairing and teaching, not solo fixing
- **Install habits gradually** — 1–2 at a time; make them alive before adding more
- **Document the 90 days** — assessment up front, retrospective at the end
- **Red flags**: "just fix it" managers, sacred cows that are root causes, broken escalation paths
- Senior engineer's value: **multiplying team effectiveness**, not being the hero

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Here's my structured 90-day plan.

**First 30 days: observe, don't fix**
- Shadow on-call for a full week; categorize every page
- 30-min 1:1 with every teammate, manager, product counterpart, adjacent teams
- Read last 20 postmortems, 50 PRs, all ADRs
- Trace one real user request end-to-end through every service
- Produce a written assessment: top risks, quick wins, structural issues
- Frame as questions and proposals, not judgments
- Quick wins that cost nothing: stale doc fixes, obvious logging gaps

**Days 30–60: stabilize the bleeding**
- Flaky tests: dashboard, quarantine top offenders, root-cause fix weekly, target flaky rate under 5%
- Deploy pain: audit stages, parallelize, cache, cut time 50%, target daily deploys
- Noisy alerts: tune or delete low-signal ones, ensure every alert has a runbook, measure pages/week and MTTR
- Install habits: blameless postmortems, ADRs, runbook-per-alert, design review for new work
- Publish progress weekly — morale and runway for structural work
- Escalate to product if stabilization is blocked — data, proposed investment, shared message with manager

**Days 60–90: structural investment**
- Debt-reduction track at 15–20% of capacity, named and visible alongside features
- SLOs and error budgets on top 2–3 user journeys — creates shared language with product
- Ownership: every service has CODEOWNER, primary + secondary on-call, escalation path
- North-star metrics: deploy freq, lead time, change failure rate, MTTR, flaky rate, pages/week
- Onboarding doc + buddy system; design reviews; RFC for multi-team work
- Team health: 1:1s again, watch burnout, protect time, celebrate wins, give credit
- 90-day retrospective: what you expected, what you found, what changed, what you'd do differently

**Key principles throughout**
- Humility first: no one wants technical debt; ask why it got this way
- Strangler pattern, not Big Bang rewrite
- Heroics don't scale — pair and teach, build team capability
- Every postmortem blameless
- Write things down — assessment, proposals, ADRs
- Measure baselines and progress — data anchors trust
- Escalate cleanly, private first, with solution
- Credit outward, absorb small things

**Trade-offs**
- Stabilize vs rewrite — almost always stabilize; rewrites take 2–3x estimates
- Speed vs process — install 1–2 habits at a time, not 5
- Heroics vs systems — tempting to fix weekend, but team doesn't learn
- Blame vs learning — team was under-resourced, not incompetent
- Escalation vs patience — don't cry wolf; data-backed escalation earns credibility
- Sacred cows — sometimes root cause, handle with allies, small wins, patience

**Failure modes to avoid**
- The savior — fix everything, burn out
- The judge — criticize before trust
- The firefighter — never improve the system
- The rewriter — lose political capital on Big Bang
- The bureaucrat — too much process too fast
- The silent senior — observe forever, produce nothing
- The hero — solo output, team doesn't grow

**Behaviors that work**
- Observe first; write it down; measure; pair and teach
- Escalate with data; credit team; admit misjudgments
- Talk to product and management as partners

**Red flags to watch**
- Manager wants just-fix-it without investment — manage upward
- Product treats engineering as executor — build relationship
- Team has learned helplessness — visible wins + empowerment
- Untouchable sacred cows that are root causes — patience, allies, data
- Broken escalation paths — document, go through your manager

**When to leave**
- Rare: if org fundamentally refuses to invest in engineering health after 6 months
- Leave cleanly; leave better than you found

**Bottom line**
- Senior engineer's job is to make the team 20% more effective, not to be the fix-it person
- 90 days is enough to diagnose, stabilize, and lay structural tracks for compounding improvement
- The win is a team that can sustain the improvements without you carrying them

followup_questions: What would change in your plan if the team is hostile to a new senior?
How would you handle product strongly opposing the 15–20% debt track?
What if you discover the main architect is the reason the codebase is a mess?
How do you measure your own impact at day 90 vs day 180?
